source.title: Globular Cluster Formation and Evolution in the Context of Cosmological Galaxy Assembly: Open Questions

accepted.question_text: Did globular clusters form predominantly more than 12.8 billion years ago, before the end of reionization at redshift z ≈ 6 and perhaps contribute to reionizing the universe, or did most globular clusters instead form later, closer to the peak of the cosmic star-formation rate at redshift z ≈ 2?

evidence.quote: For example, did GCs form more than 12.8 Gyr ago, i.e. before the end of reionisation (z ≈ 6) and perhaps play a role in reionising the universe, or did they mostly form at later times closer to the peak in the cosmic star formation rate (z ≈ 2)?

accepted.question_text: How can researchers obtain substantially more age measurements for Milky Way globular clusters, especially the metal-rich bulge clusters that are underrepresented in current HST-based samples because foreground reddening makes them difficult to observe, so that globular-cluster formation models can be constrained more tightly?

evidence.quote: What are the prospects for getting more age measurements of Milky Way GCs? It would be very useful to increase the current sample of HST-observed Milky Way GCs, particularly metalrich bulge GCs which are deficient in the current sample, largely due to foreground reddening issues.

accepted.question_text: Within current galaxy-formation models, where did present-day globular clusters form: primarily in situ within the potential well or virial radius of the main host galaxy, primarily ex situ inside satellite galaxies that were later accreted, or through some mixture of these channels that depends on the host galaxy's assembly history?

evidence.quote: This suggests that today’s galaxies should contain contributions from both in-situ and ex-situ formed GCs depending on the galaxy’s assembly history.
Bearing these caveats in mind, an open question within the context of current galaxy formation models is: where did GCs form?

accepted.question_text: What causes the approximately 2 Gyr age threshold below which multiple stellar populations have not been found in compact massive clusters, and does that threshold indicate that ancient globular clusters formed through a physically distinct channel from younger massive clusters, or instead that the same formation pathway is operating but the multiple-population signature depends on stellar mass or some other stellar-evolution effect?

evidence.quote: Recent work, however, has shown that multiple populations are in fact present in GCs down to an age of ∼ 2 Gyr, zform ≈ 0.17 (Hollyhead et al. 2017; Niederhofer et al. 2017; Martocchia et al. 2017). While multiple populations have not been found below this age, it is doubtful that the GC formation process was significantly different before/after the zform ≈ 0.17 boundary. The cause of this ∼ 2 Gyr age threshold in the onset of multiple populations is still not clear.

accepted.question_text: Can a single global model of massive-cluster formation explain the full range of globular-cluster population properties, their relations to host-galaxy properties, and the observed properties of young and intermediate-age massive star clusters without requiring a special, early-Universe-only globular-cluster formation channel?

evidence.quote: Instead of adopting special conditions for GC formation, which would imply a difference between them and younger star clusters with very similar properties (mass, size, density, stellar populations), a simpler approach would be to look for a global model of massive cluster formation. Can such a model explain the plethora of GC population properties, their relation to their host galaxy and the propeties of young/intermediate massive clusters?

accepted.question_text: The minimum initial cluster mass needed for a cluster to survive for a Hubble time appears similar to the minimum mass required for a cluster to host multiple stellar populations. Is this similarity just a coincidence, or does it arise from the same underlying physical processes that connect long-term cluster survival to the onset of multiple populations?

evidence.quote: The above line of reasoning led Kruijssen (2015) to conclude that the minimum cluster mass needed for survival over a Hubble time is similar to the minimum mass for hosting multiple populations. Whether this is a coincidence or emerges from similar physics is an open question.

accepted.question_text: Is the interstellar medium in high-redshift galaxies dense enough, across the full range of galaxy masses, for tidal shocks to reshape the globular-cluster mass function into the observed form, rather than doing so only in a limited subset of environments?

evidence.quote: We note that Kruijssen (2015) already considered more compact clusters when studying the evolution of the mass function, in a way that is consistent with the decrease of cluster radii due to their response to tidal shocks from Gieles & Renaud (2016), finding that tidal shocks are still able to turn over the GCMF. Whether the ISM at high redshift is sufficiently dense to evolve the GCMF with tidal shocks across the entire galaxy mass range, is an open question.

accepted.question_text: What role do galaxy mergers play in setting the properties of the present-day globular-cluster population: are mergers mainly a secondary enhancer of globular-cluster formation in already favorable high-redshift discs, do they make an essential contribution by assembling especially massive giant molecular clouds, or do they instead increase cluster destruction strongly enough that their net contribution is modest?

evidence.quote: It is not yet clear what the role of galaxy mergers is in determining the properties of the GC population at z = 0.
In view of these uncertainties, a detailed quantification of the contributions of mergers to GC formation is needed.

accepted.question_text: What was the initial mass function of old globular clusters: did it resemble a power law, or did it instead have a preferred characteristic mass scale, and how does the answer depend on host-galaxy environment?

evidence.quote: The initial shape of the mass function for old GCs is currently unknown – it is still an open question as to whether the initial mass function resembled a power-law or had a preferred mass scale. However, for massive galaxies a power-law initial mass function is currently favoured.

trace.notes: Mapped the PDF title page and section hierarchy from the downloaded arXiv PDF. The main open-question regions are Sections 2 through 6 and the conclusion, with explicit open-question phrasing on pages 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 18.
Extracted explicit questions about the epoch of globular-cluster formation and the need for more Milky Way globular-cluster age measurements from Section 2.
Extracted the explicit in-situ versus ex-situ formation-location question from Section 3.
Extracted the unresolved issue of whether the approximately 2 Gyr threshold for multiple populations reflects distinct globular-cluster formation physics or a manifestation effect.
Extracted the explicit question asking whether a single global model can explain globular-cluster properties together with young and intermediate-age massive clusters.
Extracted the open question connecting long-term cluster survival mass and the mass scale for hosting multiple stellar populations.

Extracted open questions about whether high-redshift tidal shocks can reshape the globular-cluster mass function across galaxy masses and about the contribution of mergers to present-day globular-cluster populations.
Extracted the conclusion's unresolved question about the initial mass function of old globular clusters.
Expanded the timing question to inline the two competing epochs identified in the source: before reionization at z ≈ 6 or later near the cosmic star-formation peak at z ≈ 2.
Made the location question self-contained by unpacking the paper's in-situ versus ex-situ distinction in terms of formation inside the main host versus inside later-accreted satellites.
Rewrote the multiple-populations threshold question to include the approximate 2 Gyr boundary and the two source-supported interpretations discussed in the paper.
Expanded the merger question to include the source-supported possibilities that mergers enhance formation, aid ejection into halos, or also increase destruction rates.
Merged the broad conclusion-level wording about the initial mass function into the more specific conclusion passage contrasting a power-law form with a preferred mass scale.
Accepted items passed self-containedness, evidence coverage, no-new-facts, source-adequacy, and schema-conformance checks using verbatim PDF quotations with numeric page citations.
